identityPage.whoAmIDesc:
Curious by nature, I started by studying life sciences with a degree focused on microbiology, because understanding how systems work has always fascinated me. But another passion took over: video games. From great classics to more niche titles like Warframe, whose game design deeply impacted me, I eventually discovered that this could be a career.

While training in game design, I found something familiar: a huge part of good design relies on understanding human behavior, what we call UX, which goes hand in hand with UI to make an interface pleasant and make people want to return. It's no coincidence that I'm increasingly interested in it. It's a field that extends beyond video games and reaches a much broader audience.

I thus have two complementary facets: on one hand, the desire to design and prototype game mechanics directly in engines, testing an idea, feeling it work. On the other hand, an attraction to a broader field, where the same design principles apply to experiences that impact even more users.

gwido.description: Explore Athara 3 with Gwido and his vehicle. Learn the rules of this world, the possibilities of each of your abilities in order to explore this planet, avoid its dangers and discover all its secrets!
gwido.context: A complete student project on Unity 3D, blending exploration and adventure in an immersive universe. The team designed from scratch a third-person exploration game with vehicle mechanics, resource management and narrative progression.
gwido.card1_sol1: Distance compensation based on viewing angle
gwido.card2_char2: Dynamic vision adapted to stealth gameplay
gwido.card2_prob1: 2 different attacks with limited time available
gwido.card2_prob2: Patrols needing to be varied and interesting
gwido.card2_sol2: Modular patrol tool in the inspector
gwido.sec01_desc: A dynamic camera system designed to provide optimal visibility in all situations, from open exploration to stealth infiltration.
gwido.split01_desc: In Gwido, we wanted a smooth camera in 3/4 perspective view. But this choice significantly reduced player visibility — they couldn't see far enough at the bottom of the screen. I combined two mechanisms to restore visibility without breaking the camera feel:
gwido.split01_item1: A slight camera advance in the player's direction to anticipate movement
gwido.split01_item2: A compensation effect based on orientation angle to balance the vision cone
gwido.split02_desc: During infiltration phases, when the player draws their weapon, they regain directional control of the camera. They can then look in any direction without moving — an essential mechanic for observing the space before acting.
gwido.text01_text: To enrich environmental storytelling, I designed three types of scripted cameras to place directly in the levels. These cameras create specific situations when the player enters certain zones.
gwido.text01_item1: Camera that locks onto a specific point in space
gwido.text01_item2: Camera that dynamically looks between the player and a point
gwido.text01_item3: Camera that rotates to a different angle
gwido.text01_note: These cameras can merge their triggers to create more complex behaviors. All parameters — distance, angle, transitions — are configurable directly in the Unity inspector.
gwido.grid04_cap1: Between — look between player and point
gwido.grid04_cap2: Target — locks onto a specific point
gwido.carousel02_label: Demos — the 4 scripted behaviors in action
gwido.sec02_desc: An intelligent and aggressive enemy, designed to integrate with stealth and combat gameplay while offering variety despite time constraints.
gwido.split03_title: A Complete FSM for a Living Enemy
gwido.split03_desc: I built a Finite State Machine (FSM) to manage all enemy states. The FSM structures behavior into 4 main states centered around the dynamic vision system.
gwido.split03_item1: Idle — the enemy is at rest, unalerted
gwido.split03_item2: Wander — moving within its patrol zone
gwido.split03_item3: Search — actively searching after losing the player
gwido.split03_item4: Chase — pursuit and attack (2 different modes)
gwido.split04_title: A Rage System Adapted to Stealth
gwido.split04_desc: For the FSM to enable credible stealth gameplay, I developed a dynamic vision system based on a progressive "rage" mechanism: the closer the player is to the enemy, the more reactive it becomes. This progressiveness creates natural tension that rewards discretion and punishes recklessness.
gwido.text02_text: To create a varied enemy within the available time, I designed a fully configurable modular attack system in the Unity inspector. Rather than two radically different attacks, I opted for the same mechanical base differentiated by its metrics:
gwido.text02_item1: Basic attack — short range, fast chaining, melee
gwido.text02_item2: Special attack — long range, long distance traveled, slower chaining
gwido.split05_title: A Modular Tool for Level Designers
gwido.split05_desc: For enemies to integrate naturally into level design without requiring additional code, I developed a custom patrol tool directly in the Unity inspector. It allows composing complex and varied routes, adapted to each zone of the level.
gwido.split05_note: Waypoints, speed, wait time at each waypoint and special behaviors are all configurable in a few clicks.
gwido.grid08_cap1: Enemy on patrol — player detection during passage

home.did: 3/4 camera that anticipates movement, state-based enemy (FSM) with dynamic vision, patrol tool for the level designer.

eom.description: Live an ephemeral musical experience by diving into your memories.
eom.context: Echoes Of Memories is a first-person experience where the player explores an abstract and minimalist universe. Its only mechanic: summoning a black hole capable of attracting then repelling floating fragments. Each interaction generates unique sounds, transforming the environment into a living musical score.
eom.card1_prob1: Creating music without the player's musical knowledge
eom.card1_prob2: Guaranteeing sonic harmony regardless of action
eom.card1_sol1: Sounds generated based on projection speed and angle
eom.card1_sol2: Predefined musical scale to always sound right
eom.card2_prob1: Providing an expressive tool without complex interface
eom.card2_prob2: Making control intuitive for all players
eom.card2_sol1: Simple two-state: attraction / repulsion on click
eom.sec01_desc: The project's goal was not to create a game with rules, but a free toy — a space where every interaction becomes a note and the player composes without knowing it.
eom.split01_desc: The project's constraint was strong: don't create a game, but a free toy for the player. We designed a musical sandbox where each cluster of fragments produces a dynamic sound based on how it's projected — its speed, angle, and interaction with other clusters.
eom.split01_item1: Each floating fragment is a potential virtual instrument
eom.split01_item2: The generated sound depends on the physics of the interaction
eom.split01_item3: No objective, no rules: just exploration
eom.sec02_desc: To give the player total creative control over their musical composition, I implemented a Time Stop and Rewind system allowing position correction of clusters and music recreation with precision.
eom.split02_desc: The Time Stop and Rewind implementation allows freezing time to correct cluster positions, then rewinding to recreate the musical sequence with exactly the desired tone.
eom.split02_item1: Time Stop: freezes all clusters mid-air for repositioning
eom.split02_item2: Rewind: goes back in the sequence to redo a musical moment
eom.split02_item3: Maximum creative precision without interface complexity
eom.split02_note: This system transforms a mistake into an opportunity — the player can always correct and reinvent their score.
eom.sec03_desc: The only game mechanic: a personal black hole the player can activate to attract or repel floating fragments. Simple in principle, rich in expressive possibilities.
eom.split03_desc: The black hole works on two distinct states: attraction and repulsion. By alternating between the two, the player orchestrates fragment movement in space — each projection, each collision generates a unique sound that integrates into the overall composition.
eom.split03_item1: State 1 — Attraction: fragments are pulled toward the black hole
eom.split03_item2: State 2 — Repulsion: fragments are projected in all directions
eom.split03_item3: The combination of both creates unique sonic patterns
eom.sec04_desc: A complete gameplay session illustrating free exploration, the black hole mechanic and dynamic music generation.

fordgt.description: A scrolling website telling the story of the 2017 Ford GT, from the 1966 Le Mans GT40 to the end of production in 2022, built around a single 3D model that reframes itself in every chapter.
fordgt.context: A personal project for car enthusiasts interested in Ford's history: a journey designed as a story, with an interface that steps aside for its subject. Designed end to end in Figma; the code was integrated by Claude.

home.did: Art direction, 12 Figma screens, specification and design tokens. No code written by me: the integration was done by Claude.

fordgt.carousel00_cap1: Intro: only the headlights emerge from the dark
fordgt.carousel00_cap3: 647: a number as a graphic element
fordgt.transp_title: What I did, and what I didn't
fordgt.transp_text: I did not write a single line of code on this project. All of the code (Vite, three.js, GSAP, animations, responsive) was written and integrated by Claude, Anthropic's AI, from my Figma mockups, my specification and my feedback.
fordgt.transp_item1: My work: art direction, the 12 Figma screens, the specification, the design tokens, the narrative direction, testing and iterations.
fordgt.transp_item2: Claude's work: writing the code and integrating it by following my mockups and my spec.
fordgt.transp_item3: This project shows what I can do: design, specify and steer an integration, then check that it matches the mockup.
fordgt.transp_note: The 3D model isn't mine either: it comes from Sketchfab (credits are on the site's “Sources and credits” page).
fordgt.sec01_desc: A site for car enthusiasts who want to understand Ford's history: the GT40, Le Mans, the 2017 GT.
fordgt.problem_text: How do you tell 50 years of history on a single page without drowning the visitor, while keeping the 3D model at the center? I set myself three constraints:
fordgt.problem_item1: A single 3D model, never replaced, that changes framing from chapter to chapter.
fordgt.problem_item2: Text stays real text (readable, accessible), even when it passes behind the car.
fordgt.problem_item3: No cards, no superfluous buttons: typography and framing do the work.
fordgt.sec02_desc: Five steps, from writing the story to reviewing the result.
fordgt.step1_desc: A sequence of 12 screens: introduction (headlights alone in the dark), reveal, GT40 heritage, new era in 2015, production rarity, power, return to Le Mans, special editions, then an interactive gallery from several angles. Each screen has a user goal written before it was drawn.
fordgt.step2_desc: 1280×1080 reference format, a two-family type system and a deliberately short palette. Text and color styles named “GT”, exported as JSON to feed the code.
fordgt.step2_item1: Iosevka Charon Bold for posters and numbers, Inter for reading.
fordgt.step2_item2: A main blue, a deep blue for large decorative elements, whites at fixed opacities, cinema black for the intro.
fordgt.step3_text: A document describes each screen: state, goal, visible elements, exact text boxes and rules about what must not be added. It also includes a proposed camera path (azimuth, elevation, distance, pivot per screen) and four families of text motion.
fordgt.step3_item1: Key rule: text only appears once the camera has stopped, so there are never two focal points at once.
fordgt.step3_note: This spec served as Claude's brief for writing the code.
fordgt.step4_desc: The code was written by Claude; my role was to describe exactly what I wanted, check the result and ask for corrections. The chosen architecture is a “layer sandwich”: background, text behind the car, transparent WebGL canvas, text in front.
fordgt.step4_item1: Anchor-based positioning (left, center, right) rather than letterboxing, so the site adapts to wide screens without breaking compositions.
fordgt.step4_item2: A camera alignment tool overlaying the Figma mockup, used to calibrate each screen.
fordgt.step5_text: Rereading the story from the point of view of a GT40 fan, then feeding corrections back to Claude to close the gaps between the mockup and the site.
fordgt.sec03_title: What was drawn, what is live
fordgt.sec03_desc: Figma screens next to the final site, on desktop then on mobile.
fordgt.grid03m_cap2: Final mobile site — Le Mans again
fordgt.sec04_desc: The design choices that structure the site, and the points that needed the most adjustment.
fordgt.diff_item1: Model weight: from 8 MB and 614 meshes down to about 1.4 MB and 16 meshes after optimization.
fordgt.diff_item2: Glass rendering: the original material looked wrong in a transparent canvas; it was replaced with a standard material.
fordgt.diff_item3: Figma → browser fidelity: differences in line height and glyph width, fixed with a mockup overlay.
fordgt.diff_item4: 3D framing: matching each mockup's perspective requires calibrating screen by screen.
fordgt.diff_item5: Responsive: adapting on both height and width, with per-screen adjustments so text and car stay well placed.
fordgt.sec05_desc: What the project delivered, what I take from it, and what is left to do.
fordgt.res_title: A site that tells a story
fordgt.res_text: A working site on mobile, laptop and desktop, with smooth animations, telling the history of the Ford GT and its ancestor, the GT40. The story was proofread from the point of view of a GT40 fan; it has not yet been validated by real enthusiasts.
fordgt.learn_item1: Writing a precise spec before coding avoids back-and-forth: every screen had a clear goal.
fordgt.learn_item2: A lightweight design system (color and typography tokens) makes the integration more faithful.
fordgt.learn_item3: Content is part of the design: a fan reads the text before looking at the image.
fordgt.learn_item4: Steering an AI for the code requires describing a screen exactly: the same rigor as a handoff to a developer.
fordgt.learn_note: Acknowledged limits: I haven't tested the site on every device and I haven't run a formal user test.
fordgt.next_item2: User test with car enthusiasts: check that the story answers their research and find out whether they would add elements or views (for example the interior).
fordgt.next_item3: Add a timeline step with the different models, from GT40 to GT (currently limited by the 3D models available on Sketchfab).
fordgt.embed_desc: The real site is embedded below: scroll inside the frame to go through the chapters, then explore the gallery. It only loads on click (the 3D model is about 1.4 MB).
fordgt.embed_hint: The Mobile view loads the site in a 390 px wide frame, like on a phone.
fordgt.embed_frame_title: Interactive demo of the Ford GT 2017 website
fordgt.dec1_desc: Only the headlights emerge from the dark. This screen also acts as the waiting screen while the 3D model loads.
fordgt.dec2_desc: On some screens the car leaves the frame (enlarged profile, rear wheel). Framing conveys scale instead of showing the whole car.
fordgt.dec3_desc: 647, 50 and 2015 are set very large, overlapping the car, with an animated counter: the number becomes a graphic element.
fordgt.dec4_desc: Free exploration (thumbnails, hotspots) after a guided story. The change of register is intentional.
fordgt.diff_desc: A few points needed more tuning than expected.
fordgt.learn_desc: What I take from this project, from the mockup to the live site:
fordgt.next_desc: Three ways to take it further:
fordgt.kf_public_v: Car enthusiasts researching Ford and interested in the brand's history.
fordgt.kf_problem_v: Telling 50 years of history on a single page, around a single 3D model.
fordgt.kf_role_v: Art direction, 12 Figma screens (desktop and mobile), specification, design tokens, testing and iterations.
fordgt.kf_deliv_v: 12 Figma screens, a screen-by-screen spec, text and color styles exported as JSON, a live website.
fordgt.kf_tools_v: Figma for the design; code written and integrated by Claude (Vite, three.js, GSAP); 4-5 days.
fordgt.kf_result_v: A live site on mobile, laptop and desktop. Story proofread, not yet tested with real enthusiasts.
fordgt.aud_desc: My target: car enthusiasts who research Ford and are interested in the brand's history. I haven't run interviews: these are design hypotheses, still to be validated (see “What's next”). They guided four choices:
fordgt.aud_item1: They want to understand, not just admire: a chronological story from the GT40 (1966) to the end of production (2022), with key dates and figures on screen.
fordgt.aud_item2: They verify: figures are sourced on a “Sources and credits” page, reachable from the menu.
fordgt.aud_item3: They read: text stays real text and only appears once the camera has stopped.
fordgt.aud_item4: They want a closer look: a free-roaming gallery from several angles, with a wheel and brake detail.
fordgt.card1_char2: A single 3D model that changes framing
fordgt.card1_char3: Interface-free intro, free-roaming gallery at the end
fordgt.card1_prob1: 50 years of history on a single page
fordgt.card1_prob3: Keeping the 3D model at the center
fordgt.card1_sol1: A user goal written for each screen
fordgt.card1_sol2: Framing and overflow that convey scale
fordgt.card1_sol3: Text shown only once the camera stops
fordgt.card2_char1: Two families: Iosevka Charon Bold and Inter
fordgt.card2_char2: Short palette: two blues, whites, cinema black
fordgt.card2_prob2: 3D framing to calibrate screen by screen
fordgt.card2_prob3: Responsive on both height and width
fordgt.card2_sol3: Left / center / right anchoring, no letterbox
